```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 85 / 25.4, fig.height = 85 * 0.62 / 25.4,
                      dpi = 150, out.width = "70%", fig.align = "center")
```

`opamr` has three parts:

1. **A crosswalk** between antimicrobial names, `AMR` package codes, ATC codes and British National Formulary
   (BNF) chemical codes. It is bundled with the package and works offline.
2. **Functions for the OpenPrescribing API**, which serves monthly prescribing data for English primary care
   by practice, Primary Care Network (PCN), Sub-ICB Location, ICB and region.
3. **Figure functions** for prescribing time series, seasonality, variation between organisations and
   drug-by-month heatmaps, sized and styled for journals.

This vignette shows each part using only bundled data, so every chunk runs without a network connection.
`vignette("api", package = "opamr")` covers downloading data.

```{r}
library(opamr)
```

## From antimicrobial names to BNF codes

Prescribing data are indexed by BNF code, while resistance data and the `AMR` package use antimicrobial
names, `AMR` codes or ATC codes. `ab_to_bnf()` converts any of these:

```{r}
ab_to_bnf(c("amoxicillin", "NIT", "J01AA02"), use_amr = FALSE)
```

One antimicrobial can have several BNF chemical codes, one for each salt or formulation, such as the two
doxycycline salts. ATC prefixes and `AMR` group names select a whole class:

```{r}
ab_to_bnf("J01MA", output = "codes")     # quinolones
```

The reverse direction accepts any BNF level, from a 15-character presentation code up to a section:

```{r}
bnf_to_ab(c("0501013B0AAAAAA", "0501130R0"))[, c("input", "ab", "ab_name", "atc")]
```

`vignette("crosswalk", package = "opamr")` describes how the crosswalk was built and where it stops.

## Prescribing data

The live functions return a tidy data frame with one row per code, organisation and month:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
use <- op_spending_ab(c("amoxicillin", "nitrofurantoin", "doxycycline"))       # England
sub <- op_antibiotic_use("co-amoxiclav", org_type = "sicbl", org = "02P")      # items per 1,000 patients
```

The bundled `op_example` dataset has the same layout as `op_spending_ab()` output. It covers national monthly
totals for every antibacterial in BNF section 5.1 from November 2020 to June 2026, aggregated from the NHS
Business Services Authority English Prescribing Dataset.

```{r}
str(op_example)
range(op_example$date)
```

The ten most-prescribed antibacterials over the period:

```{r}
tot <- aggregate(items ~ ab_name, data = op_example, FUN = sum)
tot$share <- round(100 * tot$items / sum(tot$items), 1)
head(tot[order(-tot$items), ], 10)
```

## A first figure

```{r first-figure}
top <- op_example[op_example$ab_name %in% c("Amoxicillin", "Doxycycline", "Nitrofurantoin",
                                            "Flucloxacillin", "Trimethoprim"), ]
op_plot_trend(top, y = "items",
              events = data.frame(date = "2022-12-01", label = "Strep A surge"))
```

Each line is labelled at its right-hand end, so there is no legend. The colours come from the
colour-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palette. The caption cites the data source and licence. `op_save()` writes the
figure at a journal column width:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p <- op_plot_trend(top, y = "items")
op_save(p, "figure1.pdf", width = "single")    # 85 mm wide; "onehalf" = 120 mm, "double" = 178 mm
```

`vignette("figures", package = "opamr")` covers all of the figure functions.

## What the data measure

- **Setting.** Items dispensed in the community on prescriptions issued in English primary care. Hospital
  inpatient use is not included.
- **Unit.** The prescription item, which says nothing about dose, duration or the patient. `quantity` is in
  product units (tablets, ml), so it cannot be compared across drugs.
- **Timeliness.** Data are published monthly, about two months after dispensing.
- **Licence.** Open Government Licence v3.0. Cite the NHS Business Services Authority and OpenPrescribing
  (Bennett Institute for Applied Data Science, University of Oxford).
